title: #67 Be Careful With Questions That Have More Than One Correct Answer
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton uses a "write all the factors of 12" Do Now question to illustrate how open-ended, multi-answer questions can quietly defeat the purpose of a mini-whiteboard check. With 30 students each producing roughly six pieces of data, the teacher faced nearly 200 discrete data points in the few seconds boards were held up -- an impossible amount to process -- and was reduced to sampling one or two boards and generalising from them, undermining the whole-class value the technique is meant to provide. Barton proposes several remedies: standardising how answers are laid out to make scanning faster; narrowing the flow of information by checking rows sequentially; and, most substantively, restructuring the question itself into a sequence of single-answer questions so each check evaluates 30 pieces of data instead of 200. He's careful to note multi-answer questions still have a place in the classroom -- the point isn't to avoid them, but to recognise that a fast, quick-fire Do Now check is the wrong context for them.
points: A seemingly simple multi-answer question (list all factors of 12) can generate an unmanageable volume of whole-class data -- Barton estimates nearly 200 discrete data points from 30 students in a few seconds.
When data volume is too high, teachers default to sampling one or two boards and generalising, which quietly defeats the whole-class diagnostic purpose of the mini-whiteboard check.
Converting one multi-answer question into a sequence of single-answer questions reduces each check to 30 data points instead of nearly 200, restoring the technique's reliability.

The tip isn't anti-multi-answer-questions -- it argues for matching question format to context, reserving open, multi-answer prompts for slower diagnostic moments rather than quick-fire Do Now checks.
quotes: So, the teacher needed to process nearly 200 pieces of data in the 5 seconds that her students’ boards were in the air. Impossible.
The teacher did all she could, which was to focus her attention on one or two boards and make assumptions about the understanding of the rest of the class based on this.
She could have been more clear about how she wanted the answer laid out: I want your answers written nice and big, and match each number up with its factor pair, starting with the smallest factor.
Another option is to change the question so there is just one answer.

The key point is that for each of these questions, she would have had a much better chance of seeing all her students' responses because she is now checking 30 pieces of data as opposed to nearly 200.
Of course, questions with multiple answers have a key role to play in the classroom. We just need to think carefully about how we will assess them.
